title: Parsing CLI Arguments
subtopics: Using CLI parsing libraries where beneficial
learning_outcomes: Describe Positional input and explain how it relates to Parsing CLI Arguments.
Demonstrate Flags in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Optional values.

content.intro: Parsing CLI Arguments is part of command line applications. This lesson connects Positional input, Flags, Optional values to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: A CLI turns command-line arguments, prompts, files, and environment settings into repeatable automation. Test missing arguments, invalid values, help output, file errors, and piping or redirected output.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A CLI turns command-line arguments, prompts, files, and environment settings into repeatable automation. Validate arguments before acting, print useful usage and errors, and choose meaningful exit codes.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Parsing CLI Arguments. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with Positional input; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Flags, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating process.argv strings as trusted numeric values or silently ignoring unsupported options.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse input into a structured configuration and report invalid input before performing side effects.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
